text: This lesson crosses over to AWS, where one service handles what Azure splits into Entra ID and RBAC.

AWS IAM does authentication and authorization in one place, through four object types. Users and groups are persistent identities, with permissions typically shared at the group level. Roles are different — they're assumed temporarily, not signed into directly. And policies are the JSON documents that define what's actually allowed or denied.

Every IAM policy follows the same structure. This real, minimal example grants read-only access to one S3 bucket. Effect is Allow. Action lists exactly which API calls are covered — reading an object and listing the bucket, nothing else. Resource names the bucket by ARN. And Condition adds an extra restriction — here, the request must use HTTPS. This identity cannot write, delete, or modify anything, under any circumstance this policy allows.

Most policies are identity-based, attached to a user, group, or role. AWS also supports resource-based policies, attached directly to the resource itself — most commonly an S3 bucket policy. The two can work together: a resource-based policy sets an outer boundary on who may ever touch the resource, while identity-based policies narrow what each identity inside that boundary can actually do.

An IAM role has two documents, not one. This is the trust policy — it defines who's allowed to assume the role, here a specific external account, only when it supplies the right external ID. It's separate from the permissions policy that defines what the role can do once assumed.

A long-lived IAM user access key that leaks is a standing risk until someone notices and revokes it. A role's temporary credentials expire on their own, typically within an hour, bounding the damage window automatically. AWS's own current guidance is explicit: prefer roles, assumed via STS AssumeRole, for both human and service access, over creating users with long-lived keys.
Next lesson ties Entra ID, Azure RBAC, and AWS IAM together into the access governance patterns that apply across all three.
